speechtext:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
When this bill was
last before the committee we had advanced to section 5, and had adopted all the sections to that point.
On section 5-Tag to be affixed.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The minister was going
to look into this matter.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I would like to point out
that this section will mean considerable expense to the consumers of hay and straw. In the trade it is the custom to buy this hay either tagged or untagged; when it is bought untagged it is shipped by the carload and weighed on the railway, so one can readily see the saving which would be effected in the handling cost, since each bale does not have to be weighed separately. As a result untagged hay can be sold for SI per ton less than the tagged hay. As a rule the dealers buy the tagged hay for the small trade and buy the untagged hay by the carload, very often reselling it in the car, in which case they are able to sell to the consumer at from $12 to $20 less per carload. This regulation, which will apply to all kinds of baled hay, will compel a dealer to have the hay tagged when he does not want that done, and consequently the price will be increased by about $1 per ton. I think the minister's purpose would be served if he put in a provision that it would only apply in less than carload lots.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a
letter from the secretary of the Pincher Creek Co-operative Association, with reference to this bill. In part, this letter reads as follows:
We are in accord with the placing of an identification tag on every bale but are not in favour of that tag bearing the name of the baler. The name of the grower of the hay or straw should be on the bale, then he would have to assume the responsibility for the product. We have practically decided to compel our members to do so in the future, as we realize the necessity of identifying the hay in case of dispute as to quality. The placing of the baler's name would not be of any use and would only complicate matters. I doubt whether we could get men to undertake the baling if they were held responsible for the condition of every bale, considering that the hay might be left exposed to all kinds of weather before sale. It would also lead to endless trouble between baler and grower.
It will be useless to have the weight on the tag as hay may shrink considerably if left some time in the bale. We can also presume that the hay would be sold on the tag weight, especially in the case of small lots, and the purchaser would often pay for more hay than he had owing to the shrink. We allow for three per cent shrink on all hay and set up a reserve to take care of it. Nearly all hay is sold by weight and the tags would not be taken into consideration.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the contention of these growers is quite sound,

Hay Inspection Act
that if the name of any person is required to appear on the tag it should be the name of the grower rather than the name of the baler. I think the minister, or the advisers whom he has in his department, will agree that baled hay practically always shrinks after it is baled. Sometimes there is a shrinkage of four pounds to the bale, and the placing of the weight on the tag is unsound. I would ask the minister if he would not be willing to amend this section and substitute the name of the grower in place of the baler, as the name to be placed on the tag.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I
understand that the departmental records show that this act has been on the statute book for nearly twenty years, it being included in the Inspection and Sale Act. When it was first drafted this section made it obligatory on the part of the grower to put his name on this tag for identification purposes. It very often happened that when the hay was baled it was out of the hands of the grower. About twelve or fourteen years ago this section was amended by substituting the name of the presser for that, of the grower. It was felt that the presser of the hay would be interested in the operation, and since that time it has been the presser's name together with the weight that appeared on the bale.
In the actual operation of this law it has been found very difficult to get the presser to put his name on the bale, especially when he is doing custom work and is being paid by weight. He goes around from place to place, as you would doing custom threshing, and bales hay at so much per ton. He is not concerned with what kind of hay goes into the bale, but is only interested in turning out as many tons as possible, 'because he is usually paid on that basis. Why should we hold the presser responsible for the quality of the hay? He will press anything the owner gives him.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Why not say the owner?

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That is just what I propose to do. We have found great difficulty in getting anyone to put his name on a tag that certifies to the weight, because invariably hay is sold by the ton not by the bale. With these two difficulties this act has been practically inoperative in the past. When we took charge of it two years ago, I was told by the seed commissioner that not 10 per cent of the bales were being marked, because of the difficulty of getting a presser who would feel responsible for the quality of the hay, although he might be prepared to certify as to the weight. The result was that it became a dead letter.
I have a substitute to offer for sections 5 and 6, as a compromise between these two extremes. In the past there has been a disposition to pass on to somebody else the responsibility of putting the name on the bale, because there is no other form of produce which offers itself as readily to deception as does hay. I have never bought very much hay, but whenever I did buy any I always found some of the bales to be rather disappointing on the inside. You cannot expect the presser to put his name on the bale, because he has no interest in the hay except to bale it. You cannot expect the grower to put his name on, because it may be out of his hands altogether, and he has lost control of it. Therefore, I contend that it should be the name of the owner at the time of baling that should appear on the bale. The following is an amendment which I offer for these sections:
Every owner of baled hay or straw shall, before it is removed from the premises on which it was baled, affix to every bale of hay or straw sold or offered for sale a tag having thereon plainly written and legible his name and address. Such tag shall be securely fastened to the bale and shall be of not less than one and one-half inches in width and three inches in length.
This is not a very big thing to ask for, yet it is sufficient for identification. This section is the only compulsory section in the whole act. There should be some marking on the bale holding some person responsible for the quality of the contents, and it seems to me that the man who owns it at the time of baling is the one who can control the quality of hay going into the bale. He can see whether the top of the stack, or the bottom, goes into the bale when it is soiled. He is the man who pays the presser, and he is the man who controls it. He is the only man who is likely to be responsible and hold himself responsible for the quality of the hay. I would rather have one name, and nothing else, than try to have two markings and not get either. That is the way it has been in the past.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: As far as our section of the country is concerned the law will be a dead letter unless you compel them to put the name on.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: We have a case in court up in my hon. friend's part of the country right now with regard to another matter. If we have a law like this which is reasonable in its requirements then we can enforce it.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
How are you going to deal with American baled hay? Will that hay be
Hay Inspection Act

given an advantage over our hay? The American does not have to tag his hay and he cannot be held responsible.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: We are going to enforce this act, and there will be no preference given to American hay. The preference will be given to the hay that has a guarantee, and that is what we will have if we have a name on the bale to which we can trace back. The American hay will have to comply with these conditions, if it is contended that it is graded at all.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: There is nothing there about grading.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is in the section just before.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Has the minister any information as to the quantity of hay that comes into Canada from the United States? I understand that a good deal of American hay comes into British Columbia.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Some, not a great deal. There may be some in certain localities.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I had a letter from the Delta Farmers' Co-operative Association in which they were complaining of the inequality of the tariff in Canada and in the United States. The tariff on hay going into United States is much higher than the tariff on hay coming from the United States into Canada and they are complaining very bitterly about that condition. Has the minister considered that matter at all?

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: No. This year our surplus hay, of which there has been a very Substantial quantity, has been exported to both Great Britain and the United States. We cannot deal with the question of the tariff at this time. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni will be interested in section 4 which indicates how imported hay will be dealt with as regards grading and such like in accordance with the provisions in the particular province into which it is imported.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The amendment proposed by the minister reads:
Every owner of baled hay before it is removed from the premises on which it was baled.
How can that be effected in the United States? There is no provision for the tagging of hay coming in from the United States.
If the minister is going to adopt the policy outlined in this amendment he will need to go further and say that United States hay will have to be tagged. It would be impossible to do this because we cannot control the premises in which the hay is baled. With 
regard to the remarks of the hon. member for New Westminster I may say that a large quantity of alfalfa hay comes into British Columbia from the south.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The minister might, by a slight amendment to the section, cover all the objections that have been raised. I am suggesting this simply by way of drafting. The sentence should begin:
Every owner of baled hay or straw shall, before offering the same for sale, affix or cause to be affixed-
And then go on with the rest of the amendment. That would apply to the foreign as well as to the domestic product. It would mean hereafter that before the owner offers hay for sale in Canada he shall cause to be affixed to the bale the information which the minister desires.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I was under the impression that section 4 was broad enough to cover that, but possibly it is not. Section 4 reads:
When hay imported into Canada is inspected, it_ shall be inspected and graded in accordance with the provisions of this act.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It does not say "tagged"?

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is right, it does not, but still the tagging is one of the provisions of the act. I think a reasonable interpretation of the section would cover the matter, but there is no reason why we should be running any risks.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I think the minister will find the words which I have suggested, following section 4 to which he has drawn attention, will cover both classes.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Section 4 reads: "When hay imported into Canada is inspected." That implies that it may or may not be inspected. If it is inspected, then the tag will follow. If it is not inspected, it does not come under the legislation.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I think that is right.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I would suggest that the minister leave out the word "when" and make the clause read:
Hay imported into Canada shall be inspected and graded.
If this is intended for the protection of the consumer in Canada, the consumer is entitled to protection as much against hay coming from the United States as against hay grown in Canada. If it is advisable for the protection of the consumer to have hay that is grown in Canada inspected and tagged, you cannot escape the logic of applying the same

Hay Inspection Act
provision to hay imported from the United States. It should not be optional in regard to imported hay and obligatory in regard to home grown hay.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The question of grading is quite optional wherever the hay comes from. The only compulsory feature of the legislation is that there must be some mark on the hay. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George is remodelling the amendment to clause 5 and that will take care of the point of making it apply to imported as well as to Canadian hay. Section 4 is passed, and while there is no harm in opening it up again, unless some real object is to be gained I would rather not have it reopened. It is rather an involved question and when we have safely passed one shoal we are pretty well advised not to try to run it again.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: What is to prevent an unscrupulous dealer from importing hay into Canada and affixing these tags himself, or an unscrupulous dealer on the other side doing the same tiling? I do not know much about hay, but it seems to me that our laws do not apply to the dealer on the other side. He can affix any tag he likes. He can write down John Jones, Tom Smith, or any name he wishes. If the minister really wants to protect the Canadian consumer, the best way to do so is to have a proper tariff such as the United States impose against our hay.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: We will refer that question to the tariff board.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Fort William. The hay growers of British Columbia are suffering very much from the inequality in the tariff. As a matter of fact they have to accept two dollars a ton less for their hay to-day than they would receive if our tariff were raised to the same level as the United States tariff. The minister by this legislation is increasing the handicap of the hay growers of British Columbia in competing in the Vancouver market. He is imposing on the growers of hay in Canada a certain restriction which he is not imposing on the growers of hay in the Wenatchee valley in the state of Washington. That is an added handicap to the growers of hay in British Columbia. I submit that in this instance the regulations under which the Canadian has to sell his hay should be the same as those under which the American has to sell his hay.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
There is no
difference in the regulations as regards American or Candaian hay in this bill, and the act is entirely optional as to inspection. While it
might not be proper to discuss a tariff on hay under this bill, I think that as a general thing throughout this country the farmers would be very much against a tariff on hay.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: What is meant by "every owner''? I suppose that means every original owner. The ownership might pass from one man to another.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Every original
owner would be the same as saying the grower.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
There may be a variety
of owners. Which owner has to put the tag on? Is it the last one?

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The question of
identification by means of a tag is very important. Might I point out to the committee that two years ago when we were buying some supplies for the British government to be sent to Shanghai, we put in a very large order for hay with parties near Lethbridge. The British government mentioned the grade and kind of hay they wanted, alfalfa and other kinds of hay of such and such a grade. Now if we did not have grades, how could we carry out such an order?. It is very important to have the grade established and the identity marked on the hay. While this bill is not a very exacting one, it is necessary that we should have these grades and their identity established, especially now that our export trade in hay is developing. We shipped a very substantial amount last year overseas and to the United States.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
But my point is that
there might be a variety of owners.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
We are getting at
the owner who sees the hay going into the bale, for he is the only owner who knows what the contents are.
Mr. CAHAN. The suggestion I have made is that section 5 should read as follows:
Every owner of baled hay oi straw shall before offering the same for sale in Canada affix or cause to be affixed to every bale of hay or straw before the same is sold or offered for sale a tag having thereon plainly written and legible his name and place of business. Such tag shall be securely fastened to the bale and shall be of not less than one and one-half inches in width and three inches in length.
I have simply changed the wording of the first sentence.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am afraid that
my hon. friend's amendment omits the time at which and the place where it is to be
Hay Inspection Act

tagged. We say, "Before the hay is removed from the premises." That is omitted in my hon. friend's amendment.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I say in my amendment,
"before the same is sold or offered for sale".

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
But it says here:
Every owner of baled hay or straw shall before it is removed from the premises"-

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
But the minister will see
that baled hay imported from the south is baled in the United States, and we have no jurisdiction to compel them to put a tag on the hay when it is baled in the United States or before it is removed from the premises. But we can provide generally that every owner of baled hay or straw shall before offering the same for sale in Canada affix or cause to be affixed to every bale of hay or straw before the same is sold or offered for sale a tag, and that would apply both to United States hay and to hay baled in Canada. I am making the suggestion in good faith.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
A little confusion might
arise from the words that have been used, as to who is actually responsible for the baling of the hay, good or otherwise. I think what is intended is that the man at whose instance the baling has been done, and who is really in actual possession of the hay, is the man who should be held responsible. That might, of course, be the farmer who grew the hay, and on whose premises the hay was baled. On the other hand, a case might arise where a dealer had made a contract with the farmer for the hay, and had himself become responsible for the baling of it. In such cases it would seem to me that the dealer at whose instance the hay was baled should be the one held responsible. It might be well to insert in the definition clause just what the word "owner" means. I think it ought to mean the man at whose instance the hay is baled.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The owner is the owner.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If you refer to removal
from the premises, that might place the responsibility on the farmer, and yet the hay might really be under the control and ownership of a dealer who had bought it from a farmer and was arranging for the baling of it himself.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I think the amendment proposed by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George will entirely meet the situation.
It defines the man as the owner of the baled hay. There can be only one man who is the 
owner of the baled hay, and his amendment says that before the owner offers it for sale he must have t'he hay tagged. That covers the whole situation. It does not matter whether he is the grower or some subsequent owner. If he owns the baled hay, he must tag it before he offers it for sale.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I wonder if my
hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George will accept an addition of four words, so that it will read, "Every owner of baled hay or straw at the time of baling"?

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
What does that matter?
Mr. MOTHERWELL. Any time means no time.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The only objection is that the words of the suggested amendment apply to hay that may be baled in the state of Washington and brought up to Vancouver. I am making it apply to every bit of baled hay sold in Canada.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am afraid that
what we are trying to do is to embody two different questions in this one section. I suggest that we leave the amendment the way it was introduced, and insert another section dealing with imported hay. I believe it would be better to dissociate the two things; it would only spoil both if we embodied the two in the one section.	I
do not think that the draft suggested will be as good for Canadian hay, and that represents a very large proportion of what we are dealing with.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The minister will admit that it applies to every sale or offering for sale in Canada of baled hay, and the owner must put on the tag( before he offers it for sale.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
He may have the
hay in a warehouse. Our inspectors come along and see that the hay is not tagged. The owner might say, "I have not offered it for sale yet', and in that way he would escape any penalty for not having it tagged, but if it must be tagged before it leaves the premises on which it is baled, that difficulty could not arise.
_ Mr- NEILL: How would you enforce that in the United States.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That is why I
think there should be two sections dealing with these two different questions. We are dealing here with Canadian hay, and afterwards we can deal with the imported hay.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
He might not sell the
hay; he might want it for his own use.

Hay Inspection Act

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
How many
inspectors are there of this particular class?

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
We took over this
service only about two years ago, and the inspectors we have under the seed branch, who are doing other work, are also taking over this work-for instance, the inspectors of binder twine, insecticides, seed, feedstuffs and fertilizers. So far we have been able to look after the work with the regular staff, although they are not sufficient in number to take care of it. We may require a few more to enforce the act properly.

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I assume
that the minister would not undertake a matter of such tremendous importance without seeing that the inspection was effectively carried out. According to what he has just said, that means another small army of government officials. A while ago a tourist stopped at a farm house close to the road to get a drink of water. He saw a small army of men around the barn. He asked the farmer, "Are these your hired men?" "Oh no; that one over there is appointed by the government to see that my hay and straw is properly baled and tagged; that other man is an inspector of the turnip field to see that the turnips don't grow too large; that other chap's job is to watch the hens lay and tag every egg as soon as it is laid; the fellow with the scales prevents me from selling apples or vegetables to a wayfarer by the package; they must be sold by weight. I cannot sell onions without cutting off the tops, and other vegetables likewise." This army of government officials, the minister says, is to be added to in the near future, so when the next election comes around about every fifth or sixth man will be a government official.
Now, the minister said he had got safely past the shoals and shallows of section 4 and did not want to go back over those dangerous waters again. I presume he had in mind the chart supplied to him by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). That is the trouble; the Minister of Agriculture has got the wrong chart. We have evidence of this again and again. This bill is another crack at the Canadian farmer, another restriction placed upon him, another handicap, in that every possible facility is offered to his competitor in the United States. That competitor must not be annoyed, he must be given every advantage, while the Canadian farmer is subjected to every disadvantage. If there is a large crop of hay in the United States, and prices are low,
why, facilitate the bringing of that hay into Canada. As the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) interjected this afternoon: It is better for the consumer in the case of asparagus. That was his little argument. I caught it over here; I hope the reporter also caught it. That was his retort to the point raised by my leader in support of the Canadian asparagus grower: The consumer was getting the benefit, no matter how many others were being ruined there. You are imposing these regulations with respect to tagging, inspection, and so on, to protect the person who is buying hay from the Canadian farmer. I venture to say that practically all hay imported from the United States comes in baled.	Why should	it	not also	beinspected?	It would be	impracticable,	foryou would	have to open	up	every bale	totest the quality. There	is	no chance	of
getting at the American farmer; he has that advantage. In addition, he has the advantage of entering our market at the rate of $2 a ton when there is a surplus of hay on his side of the line; on the other hand the Canadian farmer is kept out of the American market by the high protective duty. My hon. friend is consulting the wrong chart-a chart that was put in the platform of the Liberal party for election purposes, and has never been lived up to since that time. It is a variable kind of chart and of no use to guide the political ship without a reliable compass.
I protest against all these restrictive regulations with respect to practically everything that the farmer has anything to do with. They are subjecting him to every possible inconvenience and are a serious handicap on his activities. He cannot go on the market or sell a few vegetables or fruit to- his neighbour without conforming to certain regulations, and have a government inspector tagging at his heels to see whether or not he is giving the public what he professes to give them. The public should be given credit for exercising judgment in what they buy. I think I will put a question on the order paper to ascertain the numerical strength of this army of officials which the government has for the protection of the consumer and as a handicap to the farmer. I should like to know how many there are to inspect eggs, butter, cheese, vegetables, roots, hay, straw, -a whole army of government officials, appointed apparently for the purpose of putting every obstacle conceivable in the way of the Canadian farmer making a success of his business. That is what it looks like to me.
Hay Inspection Act

maintopic: HAY AND STRAW INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I do not know
whether my hon. friend was in his seat when I explained that these very sections were in force about twenty years ago; I have not yet been at the head of the department seven years. The very centre and essence of the bill revolves around the question of identification-who put up the hay. If my hon. friend had ever bought much hay he would want somebody to be held responsible for its quality. That is the only compulsory feature of the bill. I do not think he expects us to take his remarks seriously regarding the grading principle. It is conceded by all countries that if you want quality you must pay the price. The empire marketing board is gradually introducing the provision that all goods must be marked. That is becoming the . practice all over the world, and unless we want to be tailenders we have to do what we are endeavouring to do under this bill. We are trimming up a twenty-year-old measure to fit modern requirements. We have not, appointed any inspectors yet. Perhaps we were remiss in not doing so, but we thought we would first amend the old act so that it may be possible to carry it into effect. We will draft a special section to take care of imported hay which, after all, is not a very large amount. This bill went through the agriculture committee. It does not necessarily follow that it is now perfect, but that committee is composed largely of agriculturists.

That is all right; I am not objecting to that. Let me put myself clear. When Canadian produce has to compete in foreign countries, I recognize that you must take some steps to grade it so that it can compete successfully with the same produce from other countries. But in my opinion the application of the grading principle has been carried to a ridiculous extreme in Canada in our home market where there are a few dozen eggs to be sold, or vegetables, and so on. That is where the thing is overdone. I am not objecting to the proper grading of our produce sold in the old country or anywhere else. For instance, in the case of butter there must be grading

to compete with Denmark and New Zealand; I appreciate that. But the thing has gone too far at home. We are putting our own people to needless inconvenience and annoyance. Perhaps I am wrong, but that is the idea I have.

Twenty years ago
only two items of information were required to be put on the tag, namely, the weight and the man's name. Regarding inspectors, does my hon. friend know of any other way of performing the service except through the medium of men- inspectors? How should I have it. done? Reparations Claims-Mr. Ernst

Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee of supply.
Mr. - W. G. ERNST (Queens-Lunenburg): I move in amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark):
That all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor :
"This house regrets the refusal of the government to introduce legislation at the present session of parliament providing for the payment in full or in part of the various sums fixed by James Friel, Esquire, ICC., a commissioner appointed under the Inquiries Act, as losses sustained by the civilian population of Canada during the great war."
It is perhaps unfortunate that a motion of this kind should have to be made as an amendment on going into supply, but the question is one of considerable importance, and this is the only practical way in which it can be introduced into the house. As will be apparent from the wording of the resolution, it refers to what are commonly known as reparations; and in order that we may understand the question, perhaps I might take the house back to the years of the war, back to the signing of the treaty of peace, the treaty of Versailles. That treaty was concluded in 1919. To that treaty this country was a signatory. The treaty was signed by all the allied powers with the exception of the United States, which concluded peace separately by the treaty of Berlin. Three sections of the treaty of Versailles have particular application to the phase of the question raised in the amendment; they are sections 231, 232 and 233. Article 231 of the treaty of peace reads:
The allied and associated governments affirm and Germany accepts the responsibility of Germany and her allies for causing all the loss and damage to which the allied and associated governments and their nationals have been subjected as a consequence of the war imposed upon them by the aggression of Germany and her allies.
Section 232, which is the pertinent article, reads in part as follows:
The allied and associated governments recognize that the resources of Germany are not adequate, after taking into account permanent diminutions of such resources which will result from other provisions of the present treaty, to make complete reparation for all such loss and damage.
The allied and associated governments, however, require, and Germany undertakes, that she will make compensation for all damage done to the civilian population of the allied and associated powers and to their property during the period of the belligerency of each as an allied or associated power against Germany by such aggression by land, by sea and from the air, and in general all damage as defined in annex I hereto.
Annex I sets out some ten categories as applicable to article 232. These categories, with the excepution of three, all relate to civilian property damage or to injury to the persons of civilians. The other three relate to separation allowances and pensions as computed on the French scale and the question of under-payment of labourers employed by Germany during the war, nationals of the allied countries. This was one of the provisions of the treaty of peace.
Article 233 provided for the setting up of a commission to be called the Reparations Commission, and I desire for a moment to sketch the history of that commission, which had a checkered career. The method whereby the claims against Germany were to be decided was this: The allied powers were to compute how much was due them under article 232, and having made that computation the Reparations Commission would arrive at the grand total due from Germany. As early as April 27, 1921, it was realized that this was impractical because of Germany's inability to pay, and on that date the Reparations Commission, of its own volition and not as a result of the Spa conference, as suggested in the return brought down by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), abandoned the method of computation theretofore followed. On April 27, 1921, it fixed Germany's liability at 132 milliard, gold marks. Shortly after that the allied powers made a further change and decided that the amount Germany was to pay should be fixed by negotiation and not arbitrarily by the allies. However, we still had two conflicting opinions; the allied powers wanted much and apparently Germany wanted to pay little. Things went from bad to worse; the Ruhr was occupied and in 1924, because of dire necessity, the allied powers called in a commission of experts known as the Dawes commission, which sat at Paris.
It is to be noted that any amount fixed had to be arrived at under article 232 of the peace treaty; that was the only clause under which we could claim one cent from Germany. Whereas we originally intended to collect for all damage done, Germany was in the position of a bankrupt creditor unable to pay one hundred cents on the dollar. The Dawes commission fixed what Germany could be expected equitably and justly to pay. The first of these payments was made in September, 1924. The Dawes commission fixed the amounts to be paid by Germany as follows:

The last mentioned amount is to be paid yearly for an indeterminate period; in other words, next year and for an unstated number of years Germany is to pay the allied powers the sum of £125,000,000. Of that amount of £125,000,000 the British Empire is to receive 22 per cent, and as her proportion of the share allotted to the empire Canada receives 4.35 per cent. According to returns tabled in the house by the government, to date we have received under the Dawes payments, together with some old reparations before the Dawes scheme came into existence, a total of $10,800,992.91, which money is at present in the consolidated revenue fund. Next year and in the following years we will receive the sum of $5,000,000. In other words, at present there is almost $11,000,000 in the treasury of this country which has been received from Germany, and we will receive each year hereafter an additional $5,000,000.
That, sir, is one side of the question; now let us look at the domestic side. I said the method of computation followed by the reparations commission was to be based on the amounts supplied by the various allied governments. On November 15, 1918, an order in council was passed under which advertisements were inserted in practically every Canadian newspaper of importance, calling upon persons who had sustained civilian property damage or personal loss through enemy acts during the war. to place such claims in the hands of the Under Secretary of State, in accordance with article 232 of the peace treaty. On July 5, 1920, quite independent of that order in council, the Assistant Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries sent a circular letter to all shipowners in this country asking what loss they had sustained and enclosing a form *which they were to fill out and return. Nothing further was done until 1921.
In passing, I ask the house to note that on April 27, 1921, the reparations commission abandoned1 that method of computation, yet in October of the same year the then Meighen government appointed Sir Douglas Hazen as a commissioner under the Inquiries Act to inquire into civilian losses and personal damage. He took no action; there was a change of government and in 1923 the Liberal government headed by the present Prime Minister appointed Hon. William Pugsley as commissioner. The order in council appointing Mr. Pugsley asked him to inquire into civilian property damage and personal losses during the war; and he went about the country holding hearings and inviting the people to come before him and prove their claims. A

large number of persons appeared before Mr. Pugsley, going to some expense to adduce evidence, and in some cases were represented by counsel in an endeavour to prove their claims. The order in council under which he was appointed was dated March 13, 1923, and reads as follows;
To investigate and report upon all claims submitted for the purpose of determining whether they were within the categories above referred to, in the first annex to section 1 of part VIII of the said treaty, and the fair amount of such claims, and to make such findings as may be of assistance to the government in determining which, if any, of such claims shall be paid, and the extent of payment thereof.
Mr. Pugsley died before he could complete his work, and in 1925 Mr. Friel of Moncton was appointed by the Liberal administration to carry on the work. The order in council appointing Mr. Friel was dated June 19, 1925, and reads as follows:
That a considerable number of investigations with respect to outstanding claims still remain to be made and it appears desirable that a commissioner be appointed to continue and complete the investigations made by the late commissioner.
Mr. Friel completed the task left unfinished by Mr. Pugsley; in all some 1,615 claims were submitted and according to returns tabled in this house this year some 1,613 claims were adjudicated upon by Mr. Friel, who fixed the compensation to which he thought these 1,613 claimants were entitled.
This report was placed in the hands of the government by February of this year at the latest. It was confidently anticipated, and the press encouraged that anticipation, that the report would be tabled in parliament this year and that legislation would be introduced to deal with it; it was even rumoured that a draft bill was in the hands of the minister. Be that as it may, the Secretary of State himself encouraged that anticipation. On March 5 I wrote to him personally as follows: Dear Mr. Rinfret:
I have had inquiries from several of my constituents respecting the amount of reparations payable on account of their claims. One of these relates to the schooner Lucille Schnare of Lunenburg, which was destroyer by a German submarine.
This claim was presented to Hon. Mr. Pugsley when he was holding a board of investigation at Lunenburg. Are you able to give me any information about it, especially as to whether any award is being made to the owners and if so, when payment may be expected.
On March 6 the Under Secretary of State replied as follows, apparently on behalf of the minister:
I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 5th instant, in which you ask for information as to the reparation claims

Reparations Claims-Mr. Ernst
of the persons interested in the schooner Lucille Schnare, which was destroyed by submarine, and to inform you that the report of the 09m-missioner appointed to investigate these claims is now before the government, and that it will be laid before parliament very shortly. It will then be a matter for the action of parliament, to vote moneys from which reparation payments may be made.
That is not the only letter of its kind; many of them may be found scattered all over Canada, holding out a definite promise that the Friel report would be tabled this year and that the necessary legislation would be introduced in parliament. Naturally those of us who are interested in the question were surprised when on March 30 the minister made the statement that the report would not be tabled and that no action would be taken this year.
Now, sir, before we ask what possible reason there can be for delay, let us examine for one moment the nature of the Canadian claim. This country is in a position perhaps unlike that of any of the other British dominions. We were situate on the north Atlantic and our shipping was open to the menace of the submarine campaign. New Zealand, South Africa and Australia were free from that menace, and suffered practically no shipping loss. In Great Britain all the shipping was requisitioned by the state at the beginning of the war, and was operated by the state, so that this question does not arise there. But in this country our ship owners continued to carry on the commerce of the nation, a commerce without which the state would have been hard pressed indeed. It was due to this submarine campaign that a great many losses were sustained, although some are personal claims for loss of life, and for exposure due to being torpedoed. The majority of the claims are shipping claims, and it is a significant fact that of the 1,613 claims adjudicated upon by Mr. Friel, 1,493 are under $5,000' each, the remaining 120 being made up of larger claims.
Of the 1,493 claims, many are the claims of people in necessitous circumstances. In a report brought down by the government last year, in answer to a question, it was admitted that many of the people to whom we allege these moneys should be paid are in necessitous circumstances.
Does the hon. member know how much money is involved?

Yes; I am coming to that. Many of these people are in necessitous circumstances, and in some cases they are enduring actual hardship because they have not
been able to obtain this money. There is one such instance right here in the city of Ottawa, of which the minister must be aware, and there are other instances scattered throughout Canada. Why, under these circumstances, should these people not receive that which ia due them under the treaty?
Of the 1,613 claims, 752 are from the province of Nova Scotia, 350 of them relating to my own constituency of Queens-Lunenburg. They represent the losses of fishing vessels, due to the submarine campaign. There is a large number in the city of Montreal, a still larger number in the city of Toronto, a number in the city of Vancouver, some in Ottawa, and a large number in the city of Quebec.
The circumstances are that the government has practically 811,000,000 of German money, or had on the 10th of March when the return was made. The total awards recommended by Mr. Friel is $4,246,868.76. The interest to March 10th of this year amounts to $2,042,520.59, making a total of $6,289,389.36. In other words, we have received $11,000,000 from Germany; morally we owe $6,000,000 of it and we are withholding payment. Why? In an answer given by the Minister of Justice in 1925 or 1926 he said that these people had no legal claim for their money, and any payment would be a matter of grace. As a matter of law, I am willing to concede that legally they have no claim. If they had a legal claim they would have a way to enforce it other than through parliament. They have a moral claim of the highest type, due to the provisions of the treaty. Under the treaty, that money was paid for certain purposes. It is true that it was paid to the state, and the state owes no legal responsibility to the individual, but it owes a moral responsibility. That moral responsibility was recognized in England. Sir Austen Chamberlain, who was then Chancellor of the Exchequer, speaking before parliament in 1920 on the British cases, *which are relatively less numerous than ours, due to the fact that their shipping was under the control of the state, said:
His Majesty's government have given careful consideration to the position of individuals in respect of whose losses reparation will be claimed by His Majesty's government. It must be understood that the claims to be made are claims by the British government in respect of a wrong done to the state, and not claims by individuals in respect of private wrongs, and that the government do not act as the agent of any individual to put forward his personal claim. Any payments that may be received from Germany are therefore the property of the nation, and no individual will have any claim in law for any sum which the British government may receive from Germany in respect of reparation.
Reparations Claims-Mr. Ernst

, But His Majesty's government recognize that in particular cases, while there can be no legal claim, a private individual may have a strong moral claim for compensation for sufferings or damage for which it will be the desire of parliament to make provision.
A similar case occurred some years ago in a case which is reported in Queen's Bench division, the case of the Queen vs. Rustomjee. This case arose by way of a petition of right concerning the payment of moneys made by the Emperor of China to the British crown for debts owing by Chinese nationals to British nationals. The amount was some $3,000,000, and in discussing that case, which is practically on all fours from a moral standpoint with the present ease, in the court of appeal, Mr. Justice Blackburn said:
I think there is a moral claim that it be given to the right person, which must be investigated in the manner in which Her Majesty is pleased to direct, and the ministers who direct it would probably be responsible to parliament if they did it unjustly.
Chief Justice Coleridge used words even more significant, as follows:
We do not indeed doubt that on the payment of the money by the Emperor of China, there was a duty on the part of the English sovereign to administer the money so received according to the stipulations of the treaty.
So I say that there is, under the treaty itself, apart from any other consideration, the strongest moral claim on the part of these persons who have lost property or have been injured in person during the war. But there is even a stronger moral claim. This government, or its predecessors for whose acts it is responsible, appointed a commissioner who went about this country inviting people to come before him and prove their claims. Does not the fact that he invited them to come and prove their claim involve an implied promise of payment to these people? What other justification can there be in asking people to go to the expense of proving their claims long after the reparations commission had abandoned the method of computation, unless there is involved an implied promise of payment? Further, what justification can there be for expending these public moneys on the appointment of a commissioner and the payment of his salary and expenses, unless it be that his findings are going to be acted on in some respects? I said there was no justification under the treaty, in so far as the method of computation was concerned, because the method of computation had been abandoned by the Reparations Commission before the first commissioner was appointed. The Meighen gov-
emment once, and the King government twice appointed commissioners to make inquiry What justification can there be for their appointment, for the expenditure of public moneys, unless it be that a report was to be brought in upon which this parliament could act.
Let us consider the question a step farther. There is a moral responsibility on this government to make payment. Consider it from another angle, and you must come to the conclusion that the government has irretrievably committed itself to a policy involving payment, and the people expect payment. Take the action of the government in connection with the promise they made when they appointed the commission; take it in connection with the peace treaty; take it in connection with the expenditure of public moneys, and, one step farther, take it in connection with the resolution of Mr. Copp. In June, 1925, Mr. Copp, who was then Secretary of State, introduced into the house a resolution reading as follows:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to make provision for the payment of claims for reparation for losses suffered by Canadian nationals during the late war, and to provide,
(1)	That the report of the commissioner appointed to inquire into and report upon the claims for reparation of Canadian nationals, upon approval by the governor in council shall be deposited with the Secretary of State of Canada in his capacity as custodian of enemy property;
(2)	That from time to time, as sums are received on account of reparation under the Agreement of London between the allied and associated powers and Gemany, bringing; into force what is commonly known as the Dawes plan, the amoiint thereof shall be paid by the Minister of Finance and Receiver General to the Secretary of State as custodian, until such time as the aggregate of such payments is equal to the total amount of the claims for reparation as_ determined by the report of the said commissioner and approved by the governor in council.
(3)	That the Secretary of State shall, on receipt of such payments, from time to time distribute the same to persons found entitled to claims for reparation in the commissioner's report, by way of pro rata dividend;
(41 That the Secretary of State shall annually lay before parliament, within fifteen days after the meeting thereof, a' report of the receipts and expenditures under the proposed legislation.
That resolution was introduced by Mr. Copp on the 19th June, 1925. It is true it was withdrawn and it is true that the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, who was then leading the Conservative party, opposed it; but it is worthy of note that if we examine his remarks we shall find that his reasons for opposing it are these. He said: I do not

Reparations Claims-Mr. Ernst
approve of payment of public moneys in camera on the say-so of the commissioner. Public moneys should be expended only by the parliament of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Public moneys!

In other words he was asking for exactly what we are asking for this afternoon. That was the stand Mr. Meighen took against that resolution, namely, that the money should not be expended on the say-so of the commissioner. But the government committed itself irretrievably to a policy of payment. I notice the Minister of Justice remarks that I said "public moneys". I say "public moneys" because at the moment the Dawes money have been paid into the consolidated revenue fund. I am not contending that they can be disbursed without legislation, but I am contending that legislation ought to be introduced. Mr. Meighen's stand was simply against the distribution in Canada on the Say-so of the commissioner. The Minister of Justice may say: You are asking us now to distribute the money on the say-so of the commissioner. True, but not entirely on the say-so of the commissioner because there may be inserted in the act a provision with regard to distribution to the effect that if either the crown or the individual feel aggrieved by the award which has been made, an appeal may be made to the Exchequer court or some other court. It is not necessary that the money be distributed on the mere say-so of the commissioner; nor do we ad-[DOT] vocate that it should be, but we advocate that that should be the basis upon which we start and that legislation should provide for an appeal, at the instance of either the crown or the individual, to some court of finality.
That is the situation with reference to reparations in this country and it might be well to examine what has been done in other countries similarly situated. Let us take first Great Britain. Some five years go Great Britain set aside a sum of five million pounds which was devoted to the payment, first, of necessitous claims and, second, of all other claims upon a sliding scale. This was done at a time when her budget was in anything but a satisfactory condition, and I must confess that I admire the qualities of the English people who do not try to avoid a moral claim in order to balance a budget.
What has been done by the United States? The United States ease is more closely parallel to ours than any other. Only a few months ago the United States government introduced and had passed legislation providing for payment of their claims on the following basis. They had not enough Dawes money, if you may call it such, so they took some $50,000,000 of their own money; they took money out of the enemy property fund and they put it with the Dawes money so that they could pay all claims under $100,000 in full, all claims for personal injury in full, and all claims over $100,000 are being' paid in instalments as the Dawes payments arrive.
Canada is the only country so situated which has done absolutely nothing in the matter and which has neglected its people in that respect. Surely, it is time that we, having the example of these countries in mind, took action and paid our claims, not necessarily in full and perhaps never in full, because it may well be argued that the state is entitled to some portion of the money. At least, however, we ought to pay the claims in part.
In this connection in order to avoid confusion, let me draw attention to the fact that some people think because claims have been paid out of the enemy property fund, the other claims are also legally payable. The enemy property fund was a fund derived from the liquidation of enemy property in this country and debts owing by Canadian nationals to German nationals, and it is under the custody of the Secretary of State as custodian of enemy property. It is not available for payment under section 232 of the treaty, nor do we seek to make it so. It is available for payment on awards made by the mixed tribunal under sections 296 and 297 of the treaty, awards that are different in class and character from the ones under consideration, but not different so far as moral claim is concerned.
For instance, under section 297 of the treaty if property situated in Germany was taken possession of or destroyed during the war by the German government compensation can be claimed as a matter of right, de jure, apart altogether from section 232 of the treaty. An instance of that was the Massey-Harris Company whose plant was taken possession of by the German government during the war and which was handed back to them after the war in good condition, and they received a large amount of compensation. That was an award made not by any government but by a mixed tribunal under section 297. There is a certain doctor in Montreal who had in Belgium a property which was taken possession of by Germany during the war and completely destroyed.
Reparations Claims-Mr. Clark

From the legal standpoint this would not come under section 297 and unless such legislation as we are contending for is passed he will get nothing, while other people who are fortunate enough to come under section 297 are paid in full. I might cite for instance the Canadian Pacific which has property in Germany as well as Belgium. The Thompson Steamship Company had a claim for detention of ships in Germany during the war under section 297. Another steamship company surely has a moral claim of the highest character in regard to one of its ships which was torpedoed while doing business of the state on the high seas.
It is nothing new for parliament to recognize moral claims. We have recognized claims far less just than these claims. We recognized a moral claim in the case of the Home bank depositors. Why should we hesitate and delay to pay these people who are justly entitled to the award made by Mr. Friel and in some instances by the late Mr. Pugsley?

The hon.
member stated that there were 1,493 claims of $5,000 or under?
Yes.

What was
the total amount of the 1,493 claims?

I cannot give those figures
because they are available only in the report and I was fortunate to get as much information as I did, because the report was kept in the hands of the government. The total claim with interest is roughly $6,000,000.
Mr. Speaker-

Mr. Speaker, as I am the
seconder of the amendment if I do not speak now I may not have the right to do so, but I am quite willing that the minister should proceed if I am permitted to follow him.
Go on.

Mr. Speaker, after the very comprehensive and lucid statement of the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst) I feel that it will be quite unnecesary for me to detain the house at any length on this subject.
I should like, however, to emphasize the type of people who are suffering by reason of the government's neglect in this regard.
There are, first of all, the helpless dependents, the helpless women who lost their providers in the service of this country during the great war; those, for instance, who served in the merchant marine and perhaps were torpedoed. I have an instance in my own

constituenc3'- of a woman who is now seventy-nine years of age. She was invited to present her claim years ago by this government. She presented her claim. She has no funds. She is dependent absolutely for her livelihood upon charity to-day, and upon her prospective award from this fund. I have every reason to believe that an award has been made in her favour, but in the meantime she is allowed to suffer.
Then there is the other great class, the men who were disabled by reason of service in a civilian capacity during the great war. The moral claim of these people in my opinion is quite as strong as the claim of those who were casualties in military and naval capacities.
The last speaker (Mr. Ernst) has dwelt upon the policy of Great Britain. The policy of Great Britain has been characteristic of that country. It is typical of British justice. It is too late for this government to follow the example of Great Britain and to do justice in the true British style, but it is not too late for them to follow the example of the United States. Great Britain recognized that the moral claim in this regard was just as great as any legal claim. That has been one of the characteristics of that race, that there are occasions when they recognize that moral claims are even stronger than legal claims, and this they recognize as one. Without regard to the receipt of money, without actually receiving the money themselves, they advanced their own money to settle these claims, just as they advanced their own money to pay pensions to casualties of the great war. _ The United States were not slow to act in this matter when they received the money. They passed legislation this year, and it is not too late for this government to follow the example of that country.
1 should like to read some words from an editorial in the Daily Province, of Vancouver, published on April 23rd of this year:
The government, in a word, prefers to retain this money, which does not belong to it, and to allow the sufferers, some of whom have already been waiting a dozen years, to wait some more. These people suffered first from the illegal actions of Germany in time of war. Now, in time of peace, they are made the victims of an attitude on the part of their own government which can scarcely be regarded as either just or sympathetic.
The action of the Canadian government in regard to this question of compensation for war losses is in curious contract to that of the British government. In the old land, far from retaining the money due claimants after it had been paid by Germany, the government advanced sums from the public funds to those whose claims had been approved, so that claimants who were in poor circumstances received part of the money due them even before it was paid by Germany.

Reparations Claims-Mr. Rinfret
In view of the fact that this country has encouraged our people to expect payment, encouraged them to lay their claims and to go to the expense of having their claims presented before this commission, I think that action should be taken at this session of parliament to see that those claims are met.
Personally, I resent the propaganda that has gone around this house that neither party is anxious that this matter should be dealt with. I feel perfectly certain that so far as this party is concerned, at any rate, I can honestly say that we are only too anxious that this matter should be dealt with, and dealt with now. The only conclusion I can come to is that no action is being taken because of a desire on the part of the government to hold this money to bolster up another fictitious surplus.
I believe Mr. Speaker, that we may justly ask the government why provisions were made in the treaty to meet these claims, why a reparations commission was appointed, why an invitation was held out to these claimants, if there were no claims which could be enforced in this house. I sugest to the minister in charge of this department that his subcommittee should meet again, that recommendations be presented to the government, and that legislation be introduced forthwith; that, although it is late, the example of the American government should be emulated and that regret should be expressed to the claimants that we did not sooner attempt to do what the British have done in their traditional fashion, namely, British justice even to moral claimants.

Mr. Speaker, my first words will
be to express regret that we should be called upon to discuss this very involved and peculiar question on an occasion of this kind. Very often we hear someone asking, "How is it that although Mr. So-and-So has been paid his claims I have not been paid mine?" The answer is that the claims are of a different nature, and it is easy to understand the principle on which this distinction is arrived at in the treaty of Versailles. The explanation is that it was considered that any claim which existed before the war, even though the payment of that claim had been intercepted by the war, should be recognized as a private claim when the war was concluded. On the other hand, any damage resulting from the war-the sinking of a ship or the destruction of property, or any loss of that character-was considered to come under articles 231 and 232. The treaty of Versailles did not provide that these should not be paid. In article 231 it is stated very clearly that the allied and associated governments affirm and Germany accepts the responsibility for such damages. But what follows? It follows-and this is the teaching of the war-that on both sides it had to be agreed that whilst undoubtedly Germany owed the money, she was not able to pay it and therefore these damages must be treated differently from claims that pre-existed the war. Such claims, existing before the war, are not regarded in the same light as are damages suffered during the war, for which Germany is responsible, but the claims in respect of which she is unable to pay. That is the situation.

My interpretation, which is also the interpretation put upon the treaty by the British government, is that the reparation for damages done to civilians, which was the only portion that Germany could accept, inasmuch as she could not pay the rest, would form the basis of payments by Germany to the allied countries.
