Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it will be seen that I was right when I said at the outset that this question is very involved and presents many aspects that should be dealt with, not in a political spirit at all, but rather in a national spirit, in order to try to arrive at the proper conclusion, and that all parties were more or less responsible, both for introducing the question into this country, and later on for blocking its progress. Those are the true circumstances that cannot be superseded by any attitude taken in the House of Commons.
I come now to the pont where this report reached us on the eve of the opening of the session, and as I have said, not merely the report, but a mass of judgments, and a bulk of evidence requiring the most careful study, a study which could not be given to the report at that time when we were occupied with preparing the work of the session. I regret as much as any other hon. member of this house the delay to which we have inevitably been subjected in dealing with this matter, but I am sure that the house will admit, after the exposition of facts which I have made, both as regards the principle of the whole question and the facts which have surrounded it in this country, that the government could not possibly base a policy upon merely a superficial study of the report, merely upon the presentation of a report which required the most intent and careful study. I might add that that delay has been general.
My hon. friend has alluded to the United States. That is twice in so many days that we have had members from the other side of the house pointing out to us the example of the great American republic. First it was on naturalization; now it is in connection with the payment of these claims. I think my hon. friends will admit at last that all the American spirit in this house is not on this side.
We referred to that because we thought you would understand it.

But the distribution was
made in proportion to the merits of the claims as decided by that commission.

I do not for one moment ask that the whole of this $6,000,000 should be paid out. The resolution reads, "in whole or in part".

Reparations Claims-Mr. Rinjret

I will admit that my hon. friend has been very vague in his conclusions. He is in favour of going on a report that he has not seen, and it is indifferent to him whether we pay in full or in part. I do not blame him for being vague, because I know the amendment is not his. I have sat on the other side of the house and I have moved amendments myself that were put in my hand. At the same time the hon. member must take the responsibility for it. My hon. friend'3 stands is this:	I have not seen the report,
but I should accept the report in full or in part, whether it means the expenditure of $6,000,000 or $10,000,000 or $500; I am not concerned as to that; we should pay something.
My stand, Mr. Speaker, as a responsible member of the government, is that on account of the questions involved in the report, we are not yet in a position to recommend the proportion of payments to be made, and that perhaps, although we have presented the facts very much in the same way, although on many points we are agreed, is where we differ absolutely as to the com elusions. Instead of taking the attitude taken by my hon. friend, who, not knowing what is in the report, is willing to recommend anything at all, we take the stand that until we have studied fully the report and the evidence in connection with it, we will not as a responsible government make any proposal to the parliament of Canada. That is the stand we take.
My hon. friend has insisted on the fact that we have received a little over $10,000,000. May I pause here to say that that is merely a drop in the bucket when compared with the huge expenditure that has been left to us as a legacy from the war. That amount would not pay one-third of our yearly expenditure on war pensions alone. It would not begin to pay the monthly instalments on the interest which we now have to meet on the public debt of this country. If my hon. friend takes the stand, as he did, that the whole of this money must go to pay these special claims, then he can say: We have more than we need. But that is a stand that I positively refuse to take. It has not been taken in the British parliament. It was not accepted by this house in 1925, nor by any hon. member, not even by the minister who presented the resolution. We take the stand that the money accruing from the Dawes payments belongs to the nation, and in my opinion it is but a very meagre and feeble compensation for the huge legacy of debt that the war has left to this country.

Again I say, it will not be one-third of the war pensions for a year, it will not be one month's interest on the national debt. It is a mere drop of water, and should be so considered if we look upon not only these claims, which are a side issue of the war lagacy, but upon the intolerable burden that has been placed upon the Dominion by our very heavy war expenditure-an expenditure for which Germany accepted responsibility, but which she has been unable to meet in full. And surely because Germany has been able to meet only a very small portion of that expenditure we should not disregard the main portion when we deal with matters of this kind. Perhaps after all it is a lesson of the late war that we should not forget, that in modern times with all the intricate equipment that invention has rendered possible, war is not only a castrophe for the vanquished, but it also involves very serious disadvantages even to the victorious country. It may not be altogether out of place in a debate of this kind to say that it would be well for Canada to ponder over the fact that war as it is staged under modern conditions is disastrous for all the belligerent nations. And when we deal with war claims, instead of devoting our sympathy to a single class of claimants, we should not forget that the whole nation has suffered and should receive consideration.
But, Mr. Speaker. I feel I must conclude, although I have a mass of evidence before me that I have not yet dealt with.
Go on.

Now, what was the
course open to us? Taking into consideration the fact that this money undoubtedly belongs to the nation, and that although there has been delay in dealing with the matter through the appointment of successive commissioners, yet we are still without sufficient data to introduce a policy for the acceptance of parliament.

May I ask the minister a
question? He has impressed upon the house the great burden resulting from war. This being so, why is the government so lavish in voting ten million dollars for the beautification of this city and a million and a half dollars to repair the citadel of Quebec?
Order.

I do not admit that the
government is lavish, but I do admit that the government will continue to function. I for one am always ready to commend the policy of any government that leads to the

Reparations Claims-Mr. Rinjret
expenditure of the taxpayers' money on works of peace, on the development of the country along sound lines, rather than feel overenthusiastic in regard to expenditures thrust upon us by a world-wide catastrophe.
Now, what could the government have done when this report was before it in February of this year? We could have presented the report to the house and endorsed in the full the recommendations made by Commissioner Friel; but, as I have said, I believe this would not have been a good policy to follow, and in this view I am confirmed by the opinion of parliament in 192i5, which made it very clear that it would not consider the word of a commissioner as sufficient in itself with respect to the distribution of these funds. It might have been possible to table the report and introduce a measure recommending payment of the claims as awarded by Mr. Friel, and also allowing those claims which had been dismissed by him or entertained in part to be reconsidered by an appeal commission. But my hon. friends will at once admit that this would have given to the whole matter a kind of legal recognition by the government. Besides, it must not be forgotten that the amount of the claims put before Commissioner Friel totalled $56,000,000, without interest, which would mean another $20,000,000. We did not deem it advisable to throw open the whole matter again by allowing appeals. Then we could have disregarded payment altogether. In this respect I wish to assure parliament, if it needs reassuring, that we are perfectly willing to stand by the attitude taken by the British government. We do not acknowledge any legal right on the part of these claimants, but in certain cases we are willing to admit a moral right to recognition. But Commissioner Friel's report contains nothing that would allow us to proceed along those lines immediately, and therefore we have decided1- and I think our decision will appeal to the judgment of the house and also to that of the country-we have decided to give the matter further study during the recess, to look into the mass of evidence and judgments which accompany Commissioner Friel's report, in order to be in a position next session, not in any haphazard way, not basing our action on the recommendations of the commissioner, but by a very careful study of each one of his decisions, to recommend legislation to this parliament on the basis of the British award. That is to say, not to acknowledge any legal right in any such claims, but as an act of grace and on compassionate grounds to recommend awards to certain classes of claims for a certain amount
that we will best be in a position to determine when we have given the question the study it deserves.
That, Mr. Speaker, is our position. I repeat, I think it will commend itself to the good judgment of the house and of the country, and certainly it will bear comparison with the attitude taken by the official opposition, which is equivalent to saying: We do not know what the report is, we have not even seen it, but still we are willing to recommend that payment in full or payment in part, either one or the other, or both perhaps if this course can be entertained, be acceded to by the house.

That is neither clever
nor ministerial.
I am willing to admit, Mr. Speaker, that the quality of my wit is not at all on the same level with that of the leader of the opposition; but as to that I will leave others to judge.

Will the minister permit a question? He will recall that on two or three occasions I asked him when the report would be available. He will also recall that he promised the house that immediately the report was received by the government it would be laid on the table, on one occasion intimating that he expected it in a day or two. Now, I ask the minister: Does he consider that he is justified in taunting us with not having seen the report when we have had no opportunity of studying it?

I have tried very hard this afternoon to explain the whole matter. It was unfortunate that we should discuss that matter to-day and in such an atmosphere, and I am willing to withdraw from my speech any word that may have offended any hon. gentleman opposite. It was not in my mind at all, and indeed it never is, to give offence. The reason why the report was not tabled I will state. When we found that we could not possibly base legislation upon the report we thought that it was not only useless but inadvisable to table a report which would indicate to 1.600 different persons that they might be awarded certain sums which in the long run they might not receive. That is why we did not table the report. We will table the report when we are in the position to intimate at the same time what we intend to do with it.

How can the minister
justify his condemnation of us for our position in the absence of the very report which enables him to make that statement?

Reparations Claims-Mr. Cantley

I am not condemning the
opposition, I am merely comparing the attitude taken by the two parties respectively. My hon. friend (Mr. Ernst) might have moved an amendment reproaching the government with not having tabled the report, or with not having dealt with the matter. But the amendment goes further; it declares that we should pay even in full. I say that this is a very dangerous attitude to take on a question of this kind. I admit that it is not the fault of the opposition if they have not all the required information. At the same time, however, as they have not that information, surely I am at liberty to say that their stand is rather radical. If they had seen the report and realized just what it means perhaps they would be more inclined to share our views in the matter.
Is it a fact that this report has been furnished to the press or to a section of the press?
Not that I know of. So far as I am concerned, I may say that a few copies only have been printed for use of council.
I mean of course with instructions not to publish it until-

No. In the first weeks of the session some hon. gentleman put questions on the order paper and was given some information, though not in detail, as to the total number of claims, the total amount claimed and the total amount awarded. That information was given officially in the house, and all that I have read in the press has been based thereon, with comments added by the press on its own behalf and for which of course I accept no responsibility.
Now let me sum up. In the first place, reparation money undoubtedly belongs to the country; and in the second place the report of a commissioner, in the opinion of the house itself as presented three years ago, in 1925, cannot be taken as a basis for distribution of any money. Therefore, as I have said, it is our intention during the recess, when the labours of the session are over, to give that report, the judgments and the evidence the fullest care and study in order to be in a position at the beginning of next session to introduce legislation. I cannot now foresee exactly what that legislation will be, but I can say that- in principle it will be shaped by and based upon the policy adopted in the British parliament by the British government. It will not admit any legal rights, but. the government is willing to meet some of these claims on compassionate grounds and

as an act of grace. And I hope that this policy will commend itself to the good sense of the parliament of Canada and of the country.

I will ask the house to bear with me for but a few minutes. I was not much interested and less convinced by the lengthy speech made by the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) on this matter. I go back to the resolution before the house in 1'925 in which it was declared to be expedient to make provision for the payment of claims for reparations in respect of losses suffered by Canadian nationals during the war. That resolution went on to provide for the appointment of a commission. Those persons interested were asked to submit evidence and they did so at great length and at considerable expense.
I would point out that some of the people of Nova Scotia suffered very greatly. An important corporation in my county lost a large proportion of its fleet, and several other Nova Scotia companies suffered in the conflict. One company in particular, the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company, lost close to forty thousands or so of modem high class steamer tonnage sunk by the Germans. Evidence in regard to that matter was submitted to the commission, by whom an award was made. That award was made by Commissioner Pugsley some years ago and is a matter of record. I would point out further that all these vessels, at the time they were torpedoed by the Germans, were engaged in conveying material of one class or another used in prosecution of the war. Early in 1915 a company in New Glasgow entered into a contract to supply the Russian government with 2,000 cars, delivered on the tracks at Vladivostok in working condition. They proceeded to build the cars and the first steamer that sailed for that Pacific port with cars proceeded down to the Panama canal. She arrived there just as an accident had closed the canal to all traffic. That boat was diverted via the Cape of Good Hope and the second boat left, scheduled to go through the Suez canal. She was torpedoed south of the island of Crete and we lost both ship and cargo. The men were thrown into the water on a cold morning in November, their boats were shelled and one capsized, and they were two days adrift. Finally they were able to work their boats to shore at the south end of the island of Crete. That is only one case. We lost a large amount of tonnage of that character.
Several of our Nova Scotian captains lost their ships by torpedo and gunfire; some of
MAY 19, 1928	3igl
Reparations Claims-Mr. Woodsworth
them spent several years in German prisons; they lost all they possessed and suffered much in health and estate, and they demand and deserve recompense.
Now the government has received $11,000,000, and some $5,000,000 of claims are admitted. I am not now making any claim on legal grounds; no one on this side of the house has done so, though I will not admit we have no legal claim. But if it were not intended that some compensation should be made, why the resolution, to which I have referred? And why did the government act and appoint a commission? Why did we ask people who suffered losses to come forward and give evidence of their losses?
There are hundreds of cases of hardship in regard to which the minister has evidence. He has the report but he refuses to disclose what it calls for. But he asks us to be patient. We have been patient, but he has no right to hold the money. The minister should make payment and I ask him that he do so and meet the reasonable conditions laid down in the resolution, introduced in 1925 into this house, upon which action was taken by the government and a commission appointed. I do not suggest that these claimants have no legal standing; and in any case certainly there is another and a higher claim than that of legal right. I am not prepared, I am not able to follow the Secretary of State in his long' speech of technicalities and legal quibbles. I am not interested in that; I care nothing about that. I appeal to the house and to its sense of British justice. The government has received the money for a definite purpose. Let them give to those who suffered losses some proportion of those losses. And let them do it at once.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
I congratulate the government on coming to a much more reasonable position than that which is shown by the resolution as introduced in 1925. Very few members of the house will find fault on the whole with the position taken by the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) in the very admirable speech which he has made. Undoubtedly it is difficult to apportion the losses due to the war; I think that is one of the outstanding considerations which we must keep in mind. There were enormous losses of life; there were men who came home permanently disabled; there were homes broken up; there were very large property losses and there is the enormous debt which we must carry to-day. Who is to say just how much each man or each home lost through the war? I should like to urge, however, that property losses have no priority
over losses of other kinds sustained by other sufferers; the danger is that in connection with matters of this kind we should think in terms of property lost. A ship may have gone down or it may have been driven ashore on the coast; I can quite understand how keenly such losses were felt by many in the maritime provinces. On the other hand a home in the interior of the country may have been ruined; who is to say that the loss sustained by that home, which is deprived of a relative, perhaps a breadwinner, is less than that sustained by the company which lost a ship? So I think in deciding claims of this character it should be laid down as a fundamental principle that property losses have no prior claims whatever.
The Secretary of State has made it abundantly clear that any claims of this character should not be granted as by right. Undoubtedly the whole legal argument is well sustained that payments from Germany which are due in this connection to this country under the treaty are the property of the state. However, it may be very well that there are certain claims which should have special consideration. I would take it that the general principle should be laid down, and indeed has been laid down by the Secretary of State, that claims should be granted on the ground of compassionate allowance. That, 1 fancy, would limit very decidedly the scope of the claims which could find any justification.
There is one other position which I should like to put forward-and I am glad to say that I occupy the same ground I did several years ago-that is, that grants of this character should be made only by vote of parliament. I should not like to think that we were giving any plenary powers to a government commission to make large grants in respect of these claims; there should be the most careful scrutiny of all claims, and parliament should pass upon them. I recognize that with a very large number of claims and with a great mass of evidence this may be difficult, but at the same time we are all capable of judging in accordance with general principles. We should have the whole situation very clearly set forth before any definite plan is evolved by the government for the payment of any such claims.
These are matters which I hope the government will take into consideration. As yet we are not committed to any scheme and it seems to me well that now we should carefully decide upon the principles on which any such scheme should be founded.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
speechtext:
I think we all agree that in the
strict sense of the term these claims which

Reparations Claims-Mr. Cahan
have been filed and proved before the commissioner appointed by the government are not legal claims in the sense that they can be enforced against the government in any court of law. The position is exactly the same as that which arose when, owing to certain depredations of the steamship Alabama, claims were made against England and computed on the basis of the damage and loss caused American citizens by that ship. That loss and damage was recovered by the government of the United States, acting on behalf of the state, and in a similar way we have had many instances where this has been done by the British government. For instance, there is a case now pending in the United States where British citizens have suffered owing to a riot in one of the southern cities which caused loss of life. The British government may press for damages on that account, inasmuch as the damage or loss sustained by individuals can be only recovered by the British government as a government, and when recovered by that government the legal title to the sum so secured is vested in the crown and the money is the property of the crown. But nevertheless the British government have always recognized the principle that they have a responsibility to use such funds so recovered, at least to a certain extent, for the compensation of those British citizens whose loss was the subject of the international negotiation which resulted in the payment of the money.
I think the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) rests under a misapprehension, by reason of the emphasis he gives certain sections of the treaty of Versailles. He referred to certain offsets arising from the sequestration of German property in Canada and the sequestration by the German government of Canadian property in Germany, which were adjusted through a clearing house, if I may say so. That, of course, is not the sort of reparation with which we are dealing in this debate. This reparation arises solely and exclusively under article 231 and the following articles of the treaty of Versailles. Article 231 says:
The allied and associated governments affirm and Germany accepts the responsibility of Germany and her allies for causing all the loss and damage to which the allied and associated governments and their nationals have been subjected as a consequence of the war imposed upon them by the aggression of Germany and her allies.
That is a recognition of Germany's liability to pay the entire costs of the war, but that was not the basis on which the final agreement was reached. Let me read article 232.

The allied and associated governments recognize that the resources of Germany are not adequate, after taking into account permanent diminutions of such resources which will result from other provisions of the present treaty, to make complete reparation for all such loss and damage.
Therefore a great volume of the war claims which the allied governments otherwise would have had against Germany were waived. But the claims which were to be paid by Germany out of her reduced resources are set out in the following paragraph:
The allied and associated governments, however, require, and Germany undertakes, that she will make compensation for all damage done to the civilian population of the allied and associated powers and to their property during the period of the belligerency of each as an allied or associated power against Germany by such aggression by land, by sea and from the air, and in general all damage as defined m annex 1 hereto.
Annex 1 sets out the various classes of damage to the civil population. Subparagraph (1) reads as follows.
Damage to injured persons and to surviving dependents by personal injury to or death of eivilitms caused by acts of war.
It was not the losses of the men in the field, but of civilians. Subparagraph (2) reads as follows:
Damage caused by Germany or her allies to civilian victims of acts of cruelty, violence or maltreatment.
And then subparagraph (3) reads as follows:
Damage caused by Germany. . . to civilian victims of all acts injurious to health.
I am not quoting these sections in full, to save Hansard. Subparagraph (4) reads as follows:
Damage caused by any kind of maltreatment of prisoners of war.
And then the final clause, subparagraph (9):
Damage in respect of all property wherever situated belonging to any of the allied or associated states or their nationals, with the exception of naval and military works or materials. which has been carried off. seized, injured or destroyed by the acts of Germany or her allies on land, on sea or from the air, or damage directly in consequence of hostilities or of any operations of war.
This clause covered damages to property owned by civilians. Therefore when this treaty was made, and Canada, as one of the signatories of the treaty and one of the dominions of the British commonwealth engaged in the war, w'as entitled to reparations, those reparations were largely confined to loss to civilians, and there was also the payment of pensions, which

Reparations Claims-Mr. Cahan
came in under another clause. Canada collects that money as compensation for loss and damage to civilian property, and as compensation for certain pensions paid by her. It seems to me, therefore, beyond any question of doubt, that the government of Canada collecting that fund is morally responsible to see that the fund is appropriated and distributed, not to defray the ordinary expenses of carrying on the war, but for compensating the loss or damage to civilians and civilian property in respect of which Canada recovered these funds from the German state. I think there is a moral obligation. I do not imagine that we shall ever recover from Germany sufficient to pay the loss or damage coming under these various clauses in annex 1 to article 232 of the Versailles treaty.

How does Germany pay
her debt to Canada, in gold?

She is paying it under the
Dawes plan.
Through goods sold?
No, with gold.
Services or goods?

The money is received by
the Canadian government in the form of bills of exchange at the current rate, representing gold coin in this country. But I am not dealing with that.
It was natural, therefore, that the Canadian government should have asked the civilian population of Canada, who had met with loss and damage within the terms of annex 1 to clause 232 of the treaty, to prove their claims, and that they should assume it was the intention of the government to make certain recompense to them for their loss and damage, in so far as the government might recover compensation for such loss and damage from the German government.
I would call attention to the statement made by the Secretary of State on April 11, 1927, in answering certain questions put by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). In replying to these questions, the government, as represented by the Secretary of State, said:
. The commissioner was appointed to investigate and report upon claims of persons residing or carrying on business in Canada who har e been subjected to loss and pecuniary damages arising through the destruction of life and property through the illegal warfare of the enemy.
If my hon. friend had said "loss and damages suffered by the civil population", with that modification I think his statement would
be more correct. He then went on to deal with losses arising from breach of contract, and he concludes that the commissioner was appointed to investigate and report:
-for the purpose of determining whether they are within the category set out in the first annex to section (i) of part VIII of the treaty, and the fair amount of such claims, and to make such findings as may be of assistance to the government in determining which, if any, of such claims should be paid, and the extent of payment thereof.
When I heard that statement from the hon. gentleman on April 11, 1927, I assumed that to be a pretty clear statement on behalf of the government that, while they were not committed to the payment of any particular percentage of these claims, they were nevertheless committed to the policy of recognizing the claims and making some recompense in respect thereof. The minister emphasized the fact that there was no legal claim against this government, on the theory that each state itself must make claim for damages caused to its citizens by foreign states. In claiming damages from the foreign state each government asserts such claim as for loss and damage to itself, but its claim is really based on loss and damage to its. civilian population and to their property. Nevertheless, in closing his statement on that day, the Secretary of State said.
The view held by the Canadian government is that claimants for losses above referred to have no claims against either Canada or Germany.
Then he proceeded:
If there is any claim it is in the right of Canada against Germany under the treaty, and this right is being enforced as set out in answer to questions 8 to 12. This view is also held by the government of the United Kingdom. The Canadian government has under consideration the making of gratuitous payments .to claimants, and if it is so decided, parliament will be asked to make an appropriation for that purpose.
Therefore more than a year ago this house was convinced by this statement of the government that the government had the clear intention to make some compensation, which it has since declined and neglected to do. In view of the fact, as the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg has pointed out, that there are some hundreds of claimants in his electoral district, people who can ill afford that their claims should be held in abeyance, it seems that the government has been entirely negligent in its duty in not presenting a decided and considered policy of making payment to those people whose moral claims are undoubted, and particularly so because of the very fact that this government, as one of the

Reparations Claims-Mr. Fraser
allied nations, based its claim against Germany and is receiving recompense from Germany- not by reason of the cost of the war to us, because it has renounced any claim for the cost of the war-but solely on account of and by way of compensation for loss and damage suffered by our own civilian population.

I should
like to make a few remarks, not that I have anything to say in regard to the legal aspect of the ease, but because of a matter which has been brought to my attention by a person living in my constituency. This is a very hard case and I want to put on the record the particulars of the claim. The first letter which I have received in connection with it is dated December 17, 1926, from Lillooet, British Columbia, and reads as follows:
Pardon me for writing to you, but being resident in your constituency I thought you might be able to help me. I was a passenger on the Lusitania when she was torpedoed on May 7, 1915, I was in the water two hours and suffered injuries which neither time nor doctors have been able to cure. I put in a claim against the German government in the year following and since then have sent in certificates and affidavits substantiating my claim. Some weeks ago in reply to a letter, I heard from the commission that my claim had been assessed (they did not mention the amount) and that the matter was to be brought up at the next session (or now). A compassionate vote I believe they call it.	.
I cannot get to know anything definite, and as I am even now waiting for an operation on my knee, and the trouble is serious and gets worse every day, I thought perhaps you would be good enough to let me know if the .vote passes. "Compassionate vote for war claims". I should be more than grateful, as if I could show I would be paid soon, I might be able to borrow the money to take me to the coast for my operation. May I beg of you to return me the enclosed cutting, which I thought might interest you. My husband has gone away to try and get work. He was laid off the roads two months since. Thanking you in anticipation.
Sincerely yours,	.
Inez Wilson.
I took the matter up with the department and this is the reply dated Ottawa, March 7, 1927:
Re Mrs Inez Wilson
I have the honour to refer to the matter of the claim for reparation concerning which you had an interview with me this morning.
I am directed to advise that the commissioner has given this claim his consideration and has assessed it. I regret that I am unable to disclose the result of his finding until such time as the commissioner's report is made public.
For your information I may advise that the commissioner filed an interim report with the Honourable the Secretary of State, some two weeks ago, which report has not as yet been made public owing to the fact that the department is giving consideration to the schedules thereto as some rearrangement of them may be found
[Mr. Cahan.l
necessary. It is expected, however, that the policy of the government with reference to these matters, will be declared shortly.
I return herewith the correspondence left with me by you.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
J. A. Duffy,
Secretary.
The first letter she wrote was dated Decern-ber 17, 1926, and this was the reply. I received another letter from her dated March 15, 1927, as follows:
I received your letter of the 8th, to-day, and I am more than grateful to you for your efforts on my behalf. I appreciate them all the more as you are so busy. I have just been given an opportunity of medical treatment (through friends) in Los Angeles, but I am afraid to go for fear of losing the money. Could you possibly tell me if it would be safe for me to go? I mean that I would not have to come back to Canada to get the money, before my operation on the leg? I am rapidly losing the use of my leg and delay now is dangerous, but I could not go all that way and come back again.	.
What I wish to know definitely now is, now that my claim has been assesed, would it make any difference where I was residing at the time the claims were paid? If it was to be shortly, I would try to be as patient as I could, but if it is still a long time ahead, I might lose my leg altogether, or at the very least the use of it. You will I hope understand how serious this is for me, and please forgive me for again troubling you in such a busy season, but if it can be managed, I want to feel absolutely safe in going.	#
Thanking you again for your kindness, I am, Faithfully yours,
Inez Wilson.
Then on November 7, 1927, I have another letter addressed from 972 Palm avenue, Sherman, California, where the lady had gone to receive the medical treatment which she said she might avail herself of by the help of friends. She writes:
Doubtless you will remember me asking your help in Lillooet. re my claim for Lusitania disaster I heard from Ottawa that the matter would be settled, they thought this winter. Does that mean before Christmas or after? I would be very grateful if you would tell me as far as vou know when parliament dissolves and if anything at all has been done and also when the house meets again.
I never see a Canadian paper here, and they do not print any Canadian news much, so I cannot tell if anything is being done or not. I am badly in need of the money, I am better than I was, but have to have a major operation on my leg, and unless I have the money. I cannot have it done. I want to return to Lillooet when I am able and have the means. You were so good to me before that I feel sure you will help me now. Could you possibly (in confidence) tell me if there is really a chance of settlement? This suspense and anxiety is very wearing and I would rather know the worst. Thanking you in anticipation, I am, Faithfully yours,
Inez Wilson.

Reparations Claims-Mr. Stevens
Then I have another letter dated January 16, 1928:
May I trespass upon your time and kindness, to ask you if you could possibly give me a review of my ease and the standing of it, with the Canadian government re my Lusitania claim? Just recently the American Lusitania claimants have been settled and will be paid within the next sixty days. That is why 1 am asking you again to help me; I am in great need of the money; I require it for a further serious operation and I'm afraid to have it done, unless by a specialist. It is all caused by injuries received in the Lusitania.
They told me it would most probably be settled this last winter, but I've heard nothing further. If you could give me any idea of when the claims will be settled, I would be very thankful. I do not get any Canadian papers here, so I do not hear any parliamentary news. I am grateful for your past interest and remain Faithfully yours,
(Signed) Inez Wilson.
There is a further letter dated April 30th, 1928, as follows:
I am writing to advise you of my change of address, and also to thank you for your extremely kind efforts on my behalf.
Thanking you again,
Very sincerely yours,
(Signed) Inez Wilson.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the record of a case which I thought it was only reasonable to put before this house. So far as I am concerned I must say that it seems to me a monstrous thing, in view of her circumstances and the length of time she has been waiting, to keep this woman waiting for the reasonable reparations to which she is entitled. She has been undergoing medical treatment ever since the Lusitania went down. She has used up her own resources and is now dependent upon friends to receive the necessary medical treatment to keep her alive. I repeat, it seems to me a monstrous thing for the government at this time to be refusing to satisfy claims of this kind. I have two or three other cases of exactly the same nature.
It seems to me that the whole trend of the remarks of the hon. Secretary of State this afternoon was that, notwithstanding the fact that there were claims which should reasonably be met, hard cases and all that kind of thing, although the total amount of these claims was $6,000,000 and we have already received from Germany $11,000,000, the government can still go on refusing recognition to these claims, and at the same time spend millions of dollars in beautifying Ottawa and on other schemes of that kind.

I desire to say a few words in regard to this matter. I shall not traverse the ground covered so admirably by the hon. member for S6I03-202
Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst) in presenting this case, nor shall I follow the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) in his lengthy resume of the history of the matter. I wish, however, to reply to some of the observations made by the hon. Secretary of State.
In the first place, the hon. minister taunted the members of the opposition with moving an amendment on going into supply, expressing regret that this subject should have been made, a.s he termed it, a vote of want of confidence. Then he went on to say that one of the reasons why the government had not acted was because they were unable to come to a decision without a lengthy study of the report. At the same time, during the last two years he has repeatedly assured parliament that in the course of a few days this report would be laid upon the table for the perusal of the members of the house so that we might intelligently study it and take the position upon it which our judgment might dictate, but up until this time, within a measurable time of the end of the second session of the discussion of this subject, we have not yet been vouchsafed a view of the report at all. Then what other recourse is there for the opposition, when they are placed in a position of that character, than to bring it to the attention of the government on a motion to go into supply-the old historic method, constitutional, and indeed, sir, the only method left open to us.
There are certain facts to which I desire to draw attention. In the first place, there is this fact, and the Secretary of State did not attempt to reply to this phase of our grievance, that the government have in the consolidated revenue fund an amount in the neighbourhood of $11,000,000 or $12,000,000 for the purpose of paying the claims of the civilian population of Canada. They have coming this year, so they tell us, some $5,000,000 odd from the Dawes plan, the regular annual payment. Then also for many, many months they have had this report, which sets forth in detail, according to the statement of the Secretary of State, the proven claims of a large number, some 1,600, of Canadian nationals in regard to war damage. Now our position is this: The government being in possession of this fund, why do they not settle these proven claims? That is our question, and we are being importuned on all sides to bring to the attention of parliament not only one but hundreds of claims which are being ignored, as they express it, and they are asking us as their representatives in parliament to demand from the government a recognition and settlement of these claims.



Reparations Claims-Mr. Stevens
The minister made a very lengthy argument, if I might so style it, to demonstrate that this money was primarily the property of the state. That was the whole burden of an address occupying an hour and a quarter. I want to read to the Secretary of State and to call to the attention of the government the statement made by the government a year ago in regard to this matter. I placed upon Hansard a series of some twenty-five questions dealing with this subject in a fairly exhaustive manner, and in answer to question 4, the government stated in Hansard of 1927, page 2219:
The right of the Canadian government to reparation is set out in the answer to question
1.
Now what was the answer to question 1? The answer to question 1 was to refer to article 232 of the treaty of Versailles, which reads as follows:
The allied and associated governments recognize that the resources of Germany are not adequate to make complete reparation for all such loss and damage. Germany undertook to make compensation for all damage done to the civil population of the allied and associated powers and to their property during the period of the belligerency.
That is the basis of the payments by Germany to this country and to other countries, and it is on that basis that we are appealing to the government to settle these claims. I submit that the government cannot escape from the responsibility to disburse this money, through the medium of a vote in parliament, to the claimants from this source to which they refer in this reply they made last year.
I want to refer the government to another position which they took. This was in the year 1925, when the hon. Minister of Defence at that time, Hon. E. M. Macdonald, dealing with this whole question and with the famous resolution referred to a moment ago, known as the Copp resolution, made this statement, at page 4522 of the Hansard of June 19, 1925. Bearing in mind the position which the hon. Secretary of State has taken to-day, and that he is reflecting the present attitude of the government, here is the position which was taken then by the government through the Hon. Mr. Macdonald:
The moneys which come from the Dawes commission, so-called, are payable under the terms of the treaty of Versailles for certain definite purposes. They cannot be put into the treasury of the country and appropriated for other purposes than those for which they are paid.
Then he gives a series of paragraphs, nine in number, quoted from the treaty itself, and indicates their purpose, to which the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. 
Cahan) and other hon. gentlemen have referred. Now our point is this: The Dominion government having received these millions of dollars, more than double the amount required, and with another $5,000,000 coming along this year, and another $5,000,000 or $6,000,000 payable next year, we submit that these claims should be satisfied.	.
The hon. Secretary of State says: We want carefully to study the findings of Mr. Friel; we are not satisfied that those findings are fair, and we want to study them carefully, and next session we may bring in a measure to pay these claims. A year ago the minister had a still different view. Speaking officially for the government a year ago, he said, and I am quoting from page 2219 of Hansard:
The policy of the government will be decided when the reparation commissioner has completed his report.
It may be said that that was a vague answer. At the time I did not take it as such, because the minister had repeatedly said, in answer to questions on the orders of the day, that they were expecting the report hourly, and the moment it was received action would be taken on it. Furthermore, the government had itself asked for and received an interim report, which dealt with what might be called non-contentious claims, which were obviously fair and should be settled. The government had that interim report in its hands over a year ago, but no action has been taken. How can the government justly complain of the position that the opposition is now taking in regard to the delay in introducing justifiable measures on behalf of these claimants?
What we are asking is this. In the first place, we ask that the report be laid on the table. This may seem a strong statement, but I make it advisedly: I submit that the government is guilty of a dereliction of duty to this house, indeed it is guilty of a lack of respect, in not long ago tabling the report. The report is not secret; the government must produce it sooner or later in its present form. The government may attach to it whatever it likes, but the parliament of Canada is entitled to the report. The minister says: Oh, what is the use of laying the report on the table; it is simply a long string of names and of figures. Well, give us the names and the figures. But, I submit, Mr. Speaker, that parliament is entitled to the report; and, furthermore, the government is open to severe censure in having suppressed the report up to this time. The report has been in the hands of the government since before the opening

Reparations Claims-Mr. Stevens
of the session, according to the Secretary of State. We have gone through the whole session with repeated requests and references to reparations, and in face of the government declaration of last session I repeat that the failure to table the report is evidence of disrespect to parliament. So we ask that the report be tabled, and we have the right to demand that it be tabled before the close of this session. And, further, we have the right to ask for action on the report. In short, we want the report, and we want action on it. We are convinced from what we are able to learn, not only from the meagre knowledge we can glean from the government about the situation in Canada, but from parallel conditions in the United Sates, in Great Britain, in France and other countries- we are convinced, I say, that some at least of these claims may justly be paid. We know that in a large number of cases the failure to make payment has caused suffering similar to that to which my hon. friend from Cariboo (Mr. Fraser) brought to the attention of the house a moment ago. The case he mentioned is only one of hundreds in this country involving actual privation and suffering. I have in my room a letter from a lady, over eighty years of age, who is suffering severe privation from the lack of funds due to losses during the war incurred through the sinking of the Lusitania or a similar incident. My hon. leader reminds me that she lost her husband, a master mariner. He knows the case as well as I do. These are pathetic cases, there are hundreds of them throughout the country, and we submit that these minor claims

minor in respect to the amount of money involved-should be settled. It may be that in some of the large claims -I understand there are one or two of over a million dollars-time should be taken to scrutinize them carefully. If there are such cases, by all means scrutinize them with the greatest of care; no one objects to that; but we do object to the holding up of claims by individuals who are suffering privation while the government coolly takes time to look into these other matters.
Why is not the government prepared to take action this session? I confess frankly to the Prime Minister and his colleagues that I cannot understand it. I cannot find any conceivable excuse for the delay, and I have studied earnestly to find an excuse. The Secretary of State gave us none this afternoon. He intimated that the government wants to scrutinize the claims. I submit to him that between January and to-day there has been ample time to scrutinize a great many of
these claims. Indeed, the major portion of them have been in his hands for two years on the interim report made by Mr. Friel. They have been in his hands long enough for him to go over the investigation three or four times. These claims could very properly be paid. If any of them are of a doubtful character, hold them in abeyance. But let us at least have the privilege of examining the report. Then we will be in a position to judge whether the minister is making a fair interpretation of the report when he says that it is so delicate -and so intricate that he must take another year to scrutinize it and determine what action should be taken. I wonder, is it the purpose of the government to look into this report and scrutinize the findings with the expectation that some of the claims may be increased? Or does the government wish to decrease them? Is it the intention to decrease these claims or to increase them? Why the delay? It is rather significant that next session we will be one year nearer an election than we are to-day. The minister asks: Why should we make a political issue out of this, because we ask for a redress of the grievances of the people on going into supply. I ask him now, since he has indulged in implications, am I not justified in drawing this inference, that inasmuch as next session will carry us much nearer the time of an election, is not the government at least inviting designing persons to press for the payment of their claims in return for political support? That may not be so, but I say, is it not a fair inference?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, most
unfair.

Then I say to the Prime Minister it is most unfair for him to deny us our right to see that report. It is most unfair for him to deny the citizens of Canada payment of their just claims out of the moneys which the government has wrongfully put into the consolidated fund, according to an official declaration on behalf of the government by a minister of the crown from his place in the house. It is he whom I quote in support of my contention.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State suggests that the report is for his personal study. I submit that it is not for his personal study. He has no more right to that report than I have. It is a report to parliament, a report for this house to consider and determine what action shall be taken. Why, the ministry itself last session and this session has said, indeed the Secretary of State has repeated the language this afternoon, that

Reparations Claims-Mr. Stevens
the only way effect can be given to the report is by a vote in parliament, by putting in the estimates an item to deal with the claims. It is obvious that the report is the property of parliament, and it is equally obvious that we are denied rightful access to our own property. The minister has no right to say that the report is for his own personal study.
Then the minister made this statement: he said that an appeal to the court would have given a legal air to this matter. That is to say, if they had appealed from Commissioner Friel to the court a legal air would have been given to these claims. Why are the government afraid of "a legal air"? A little while ago they said that there was no legal point at all at issue, that it was an act of grace. While I am not a lawyer I do not agree with that. I believe that under the terms of the treaty these people have an absolute legal claim against this fund-a claim which they cannot enforce because the funds are in possession of the government.
Another statement the minister made was that this report could not be taken as a basis of any payments. But I find, in his replies of a year ago, that he declares that the intention of the commission and of the report was to secure the bases upon which payment could be made. To-day however he says that the report cannot be taken as a basis of payment. I reiterate that what we are asking for is the report, which is the property of parliament, and action upon that report this session.
On motion of Mr. Bennett the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the house adjourned at 5.55 p.m.
